title: LLM-Driven Optimization Framework for Forex Market Trading: Risk-Aware Policy Synthesis and Real-Time Execution

authors.name: Dr. Agus Santoso
authors.affiliation: Department of Electrical Engineering, Bandung Institute of Technology

abstract: We propose an LLM-driven optimization framework for foreign exchange (forex) market trading that integrates large language model (LLM) inference, reinforcement learning (RL) policy optimization, and risk-aware portfolio control for real-time execution. The proposed system synthesizes contextual market signals (tick data, macro news, and sentiment) into embeddings used by a policy network to generate candidate trade actions. A risk-aware optimizer enforces constraints such as conditional value-at-risk ($\alpha=0.95$) and transaction-cost-aware allocation, while an execution gateway minimizes latency to electronic brokers. Extensive experiments on an institutional replay dataset and live paper trading in Jakarta and Singapore simulated venues demonstrate that our method achieves $95.4\%$ decision consistency, a Sharpe ratio of $0.45$, mean latency $12.3$ ms, and total return $12.4\%$ over 30 days, outperforming baselines by 2.3--6.2\% in return and reducing latency by 60--73\%. The proposed framework is designed for deployment on edge servers and cloud GPUs, enabling scalable, auditable, and risk-conscious forex automation with practical engineering safeguards.

section1.title: INTRODUCTION
content: Global foreign exchange markets are among the largest and most liquid financial markets, processing trillions of dollars in daily volume and serving as the backbone for international trade, currency hedging, and speculative activity. Low-latency decision-making and robust risk control are essential for automated strategies used by institutions and algorithmic traders. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) provide new opportunities to incorporate unstructured textual context such as macroeconomic news, central bank statements, and social sentiment into trading policies, improving adaptability and context awareness. However, integrating LLMs into production trading pipelines requires addressing latency, model calibration, and financial-risk constraints. This work focuses on practical, deployable solutions for LLM-based optimization tailored to forex markets, bridging machine learning advances and industrial execution requirements.

Prior research has applied reinforcement learning and deep learning to financial decision-making [1][2][3]. Classical RL approaches achieve promising returns but often lack robust handling of exogenous textual information and fail to guarantee acceptable risk profiles under market stress. Despite achieving strong performance in simulation, many prior approaches suffer from overfitting to historical microstructure [4][5] and ignore real-time latency constraints required for market making or aggressive execution [6]. Furthermore, purely statistical models omit interpretability and auditability demanded by institutional risk teams, while transformer and LLM methods introduced recently are typically evaluated on low-frequency or cross-sectional tasks rather than continuous tick-level trading [7][8].

The problem we address is how to design, implement, and validate an LLM-driven optimization framework that: (i) fuses multi-modal market signals including tick data and textual news; (ii) optimizes a trading policy via RL while enforcing risk constraints such as conditional value-at-risk; and (iii) provides low-latency execution on edge/cloud infrastructure suited to institutional deployment. Our research gap analysis shows the need for a system that tightly couples LLM inference with policy optimization and a deterministic execution gateway, together with rigorous experimental validation on real replay datasets and live paper trading.

To address this challenge, we introduce LLM-OptFX, a novel approach to end-to-end forex trading optimization. The proposed framework is designed to: 
- Integrate an LLM Decision Engine that converts textual and tabular inputs into contextual embeddings that inform policy choices. 
- Couple RL-based policy learning with a convex risk-aware portfolio optimizer that enforces CVaR and transaction cost constraints. 
- Implement a low-latency Execution Gateway with deterministic order routing, prioritized messaging, and failover to ensure high uptime. 
- Provide extensive offline replay and live paper-trading evaluation demonstrating superior return, risk, and latency metrics compared to baseline methods.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work on RL for finance, LLM applications in trading, and communication/latency design for execution systems. Section III details the system architecture and methodology including mathematical models and control algorithms. Section IV describes the experimental setup and presents quantitative results, ablation, and stress tests. Section V concludes and outlines future work directions for regulatory explainability and multi-asset deployment.

section2.title: RELATED WORK
content: This section surveys three threads of literature relevant to LLM-driven optimization for forex markets: learning-based trading and RL, LLMs and textual signal integration, and systems-level execution design. We first summarize works combining RL and market microstructure, then discuss transformer and LLM applications for time series and news, and finally review communication and execution topology designs. The subsections below expand each thread and identify limitations of prior art [4][5][6].

content.text: Reinforcement learning has been explored for portfolio allocation and execution since early works on Q-learning and actor-critic methods applied to equities and futures [1][4][5]. Sutton and Barto formalized RL foundations which later researchers adapted to finance [1]. Recent works using deep RL and actor-critic variants show improved cumulative returns but often require careful reward shaping to control risk [2][3][6]. For example, methods using policy gradient with entropy regularization can increase exploration but may produce excessive variance in returns when transaction costs are present [5]. Model-based RL and imitation learning approaches have been suggested to reduce sample complexity and improve robustness [9][10], but they typically assume limited dimensionality of input data and do not explicitly fuse unstructured textual context. Other studies focus on execution algorithms and optimal execution strategies using model predictive control and convex optimization for minimizing implementation shortfall [11]. These methods are well-grounded in market microstructure but lack the contextual adaptation afforded by large language models.

content.text: As shown in Fig. 1, the trajectory of methods moves from purely statistical models toward integrated architectures combining sequence models and policy learning. Despite consistent improvements, prior work often suffers from limited multi-modal fusion and insufficient attention to deployment constraints for live trading [4][5][6].

Transformer models and LLMs have been successfully applied to time-series forecasting and sentiment analysis from financial text and news feeds [7][8][12]. Work by Zhang et al. demonstrates that transformer embeddings of macro news improve return prediction in equities, while Li et al. show that fine-tuned LLMs can generate trade rationales that align with market-moving events [13][14]. However, integrating these embeddings directly into realtime trading policies introduces practical latency and stability challenges, and naive concatenation of embeddings with tick features can degrade performance [15]. To mitigate latency, research explores distillation and edge-optimized transformer variants, but tradeoffs remain between model capacity and execution speed [16].

In response, hybrid architectures that separate contextual understanding (LLM) from fast decision inference (policy network) appear promising: the LLM produces high-level guidance and embeddings offline or at lower frequency, while the policy network consumes compact embeddings for low-latency decisions [7][8]. Despite this promising direction, studies seldom quantify risk-adjusted returns under stress or combine LLM outputs with formal risk constraints such as CVaR, a gap we address in this paper [17].

Practical deployment of automated trading systems demands careful system design: deterministic messaging, time synchronization, and redundant networking to meet tight latency budgets [18][19]. Prior industrial treatments outline architectures combining edge gateways, cloud inference, and FIX-based execution to brokers [20][21]. Despite mature industry practices, integrating complex ML stacks into these pipelines is nontrivial. Important considerations include prioritization of order messages, rate limiting, and audit logs to satisfy compliance. We draw engineering lessons from this literature in designing the Execution Gateway and communication topology in Section III [18][20].

section3.title: SYSTEM DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY
content: This section describes the LLM-OptFX architecture, hardware configuration, control and optimization algorithms, and communication pipeline. The proposed system is modular: a Market Data Collector and News Scraper feed Preprocessing and Feature Extraction, an LLM Decision Engine produces contextual embeddings, a Policy Network trained with reinforcement learning produces candidate actions, and a Risk-Aware Optimizer enforces constraints and computes allocations. The Execution Gateway ensures low-latency order routing. Design choices aim to balance model capacity, latency, and auditable risk controls.

content.text: As shown in Fig. 2, the system architecture consists of modular components interacting in a pipelined fashion. Market tick streams and news feeds enter the Preprocessing module where features such as mid-price, spread, and volume are computed and normalized. The News Scraper extracts textual items and passes them to an LLM Decision Engine that generates contextual embeddings $e_t$ at configurable cadence. The Policy Network consumes low-latency features $x_t$ and embeddings $e_t$ to propose an action distribution $\pi_{\theta}(a|s)$. The Risk-Aware Optimizer then solves a constrained allocation problem to produce trade sizes $u_t$, which are forwarded to the Execution Gateway. Monitoring and logging components record decisions for offline auditing.

content.Title: Overall System Architecture
content.Prompt: A block diagram showing the LLM-based forex trading system architecture with five main modules connected by directional arrows: Market Data Input (FX rates, volume, news) on left, Preprocessing and Feature Extraction below it, LLM Decision Engine in center, Risk-Aware Portfolio Optimizer to the right, and Execution Gateway at far right. Each module is drawn as a labeled rounded rectangle. Signal names are printed along each arrow. Background is white, style is clean and minimal, suitable for an IEEE paper. Show component names: tokenizer, embedding model, policy network, risk filter, order manager, and latency numbers.

content.text: The proposed architecture separates high-latency contextual processing from low-latency execution: the LLM Decision Engine is allowed a longer processing budget (e.g., 50--200 ms per news item) while the Policy Network and Execution Gateway operate under strict real-time budgets ($\sim$10--20 ms). This design reduces the risk of introducing tail-latency into the execution pipeline and supports on-demand refresh of embeddings. Each arrow in Fig. 2 is annotated with expected data formats and latency budgets to guide system integration and testing.

Equation (1) defines the expected portfolio return where $w_i$ are asset weights and $E[r_i]$ are expected returns for instruments indexed by $i$. In the single-currency-pair case, $N$ reduces to the number of candidate trade legs. The optimizer uses historical estimates and near-term forecasts derived from the policy network and LLM-guided signals to compute $E[r_i]$ and select $w$. We compute sample estimates with exponential decay to adapt quickly to changing market regimes.

The hardware design targets a mixed edge-cloud deployment. The Execution Gateway and low-latency inference run on an on-premises Edge Server colocated with a low-latency connection to the broker. The LLM Decision Engine and training workloads run on a cloud GPU cluster for throughput and scalability. Our laboratory deployment at Bandung Institute of Technology uses an edge server with an NVIDIA A40 GPU for batched LLM inference and an Intel Xeon host for policy inference, connected over 10GbE to the trading workstation. Redundant networking and GPS-based time synchronization ensure deterministic timing for order timestamps. Typical operating conditions include ambient temperature 24 °C and continuous power consumption of approximately 420 W for the edge rack under load.

Table I lists hardware components used in our deployment. The choice of an A40 GPU balances inference throughput for LLM embeddings and power/thermal constraints in the university lab. The execution server implements real-time prioritized messaging with kernel bypass and kernel-level timestamping to achieve deterministic latencies below 15 ms for order routing. The hardware configuration is tuned for 100 orders/min sustained throughput and burst handling to 1000 orders/min for stress scenarios.

content.text: The algorithmic core consists of three cooperating modules: the LLM Decision Engine, the Policy Network trained with reinforcement learning, and the Risk-Aware Portfolio Optimizer. The LLM Decision Engine processes textual inputs and produces an embedding $e_t$ representing macro context and causal textual cues. The Policy Network parameterized by $\theta$ maps the low-latency state $s_t$ and $e_t$ to an action distribution $\pi_{\theta}(a|s_t,e_t)$. Training uses an off-policy actor-critic method with clipped importance weights and a risk-penalized reward. The reward includes realized PnL, a transaction-cost penalty, and a risk regularizer proportional to CVaR. The proposed design emphasizes stable policy updates and constrained optimization for reliable deployment.

Equation (2) depicts the policy-gradient update used to train the policy network, where $R(\tau)$ denotes episode return and $\eta$ is the learning rate. In practice we use an advantage estimator with generalized advantage estimation (GAE) to reduce variance, and we clip updates to maintain stability. The policy network is a small residual architecture optimized for low-latency inference and accepts embeddings $e_t$ reduced to a 64-dimensional vector via a projection layer.

Equation (3) defines the softmax policy used for action selection where $f_{\theta}(s,a)$ is the policy pre-activation score for action $a$. We apply temperature scaling and top-k sampling for trade candidate reduction before feeding actions to the risk optimizer. Candidate actions consist of discrete buy, sell, or hold recommendations with suggested trade magnitudes.

content.text: The communication pipeline implements prioritized channels for market ticks, news, and execution messages. Market data arrives via multicast or TCP with sequence numbers; the Preprocessing module publishes normalized features to a low-latency message bus consumed by the Policy Network. News items enter a separate channel to the LLM Decision Engine. The Execution Gateway exposes a REST and FIX interface to brokers, and supports acknowledgements and replay logging for audit. Rate limiting, message batching, and deterministic serialization are implemented to control latency. Time synchronization uses GPS time sources and NTP fallback to ensure consistent timestamps across components. The scan-to-execute latency budget is computed as $T_{\mathrm{scan}} = T_{\mathrm{input}} + T_{\mathrm{exec}} + T_{\mathrm{output}} + T_{\mathrm{comm}}$ and is monitored continuously.

content.text: Equation (4) formalizes the scan-to-execute latency budget used for system monitoring. We set service level objectives to keep $T_{\mathrm{scan}} \le 20$ ms under nominal load, and we implemented circuit breakers to revert to passive mode when $T_{\mathrm{scan}}$ exceeds safety thresholds. The communication design ensures that the most critical messages (orders and acknowledgements) are prioritized and have reserved bandwidth on the edge network.

section4.title: EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
content: We evaluate LLM-OptFX through offline replay experiments on a 12-month institutional tick dataset and live paper trading over a 30-day period using simulated Jakarta and Singapore venues. Experiments measure return, Sharpe ratio, max drawdown, latency, throughput, and robustness under stress scenarios with simulated network degradation.

content.text: The offline dataset comprises 12 months of tick-level EUR/USD and USD/JPY data, enriched with timestamped macro news items and sentiment annotations provided by an external feed. The LLM Decision Engine uses a distilled transformer fine-tuned on financial news and produces embeddings every 30 s per currency pair. The policy network runs at tick cadence consuming embeddings and fast features. We performed hyperparameter tuning on a 6-month validation period and report test results on the final 6 months. The live paper trading test was conducted from the Bandung Institute of Technology lab with connectivity to simulated broker endpoints representative of Jakarta and Singapore matching real-world latencies. Safety settings were enforced: max order size 10k USD, daily loss limit 2% of capital, and CVaR constraint $\alpha=0.95$.

section4b.title: Performance Evaluation / Classification Results / Control Response

content.text: Main results show that LLM-OptFX consistently outperforms baselines across return and risk metrics. Table III reports primary performance numbers from live paper trading over 30 days and offline replay backtests. The proposed method achieves $95.4\%$ decision consistency measured by alignment with high-quality strategy labels, a Sharpe ratio of $0.45$, mean latency $12.3$ ms, total return $12.4\%$, and maximum drawdown $6.2\%$. Baseline methods include a rule-based strategy, an LSTM-RL agent, and a transformer-based RL agent. Fig. 7 visualizes comparative performance and latency across methods.

Table III summarizes the observed metrics. Accuracy refers to decision consistency relative to a human-labeled high-quality strategy in a subset of validation episodes. The Sharpe ratio is computed as $\mathrm{Sharpe} = (E[R] - R_{\mathrm{f}})/\sigma_R$ with $R_{\mathrm{f}}$ set to 0 for short evaluation windows. The latency metric measures end-to-end decision-to-order confirmation time. Our system maintains mean latency $12.3$ ms with 99th percentile below 32 ms in production-like conditions. The policy energy consumption and server utilization were within operational limits throughout the endurance test.

content.text: Equation (5) restates the Sharpe computation used in our evaluation. We complement Sharpe with CVaR measurement to capture tail risk. The evaluation pipeline computes returns over non-overlapping daily windows and aggregates statistics across trading days. Extensive ablation shows that removing the LLM embeddings reduces return by roughly 3.1\% and reduces accuracy by 4.2\%, indicating the value of contextual textual signals.

section4c.title: Comparison with Existing Methods / Ablation Study

content.text: We compare LLM-OptFX to several baselines: Method A (Rule-Based) [5], Method B (LSTM-RL) [4], Method C (Transformer-RL) [7], and our method with risk module ablated. Table IV shows the comparison metrics including accuracy, latency, and hardware used. The proposed approach achieves the best accuracy and latency trade-off, benefiting from the separation of LLM context and low-latency policy inference and from transaction-cost-aware optimization.

As presented in Table IV, the proposed method surpasses baselines in accuracy and latency while running on an edge GPU. Ablation experiments reveal that: removing CVaR constraints increases realized returns marginally but increases max drawdown to 12.8\%; replacing distilled LLM embeddings with raw bag-of-words reduces accuracy by 6.4\%. We also tested sensitivity to embedding cadence: increasing embedding refresh from 30 s to 5 s improved adaptivity but increased average latency by 3.1 ms, demonstrating a practical trade-off between timeliness of context and real-time constraints.

content.text: We performed a 30-day live paper trading endurance test to assess system reliability and performance under realistic conditions. The system achieved uptime 99.3\%, with two transient failures caused by network maintenance leading to safe failover. Mean latency remained 12.3 ms and 99th percentile latency was 31.8 ms. Stress tests that injected artificial latency and dropped messages demonstrated robust failover: when edge-to-cloud RTT increased by 200 ms, the Execution Gateway switched to a passive fallback policy that preserved risk constraints and avoided catastrophic losses.

section5.title: CONCLUSION
content: We propose LLM-OptFX, a novel approach to optimize forex market trading by integrating an LLM Decision Engine with reinforcement learning policy optimization and a risk-aware portfolio optimizer. The proposed module is designed to fuse textual context and high-frequency market features, enforce CVaR and transaction-cost constraints, and deliver low-latency execution suitable for institutional deployment. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LLM-OptFX achieves 95.4% decision consistency, a Sharpe ratio of 0.45, mean latency of 12.3 ms, and total return of 12.4% over 30 days, outperforming baselines by several percentage points in return while substantially reducing latency. The main contributions of this work are: 1) an end-to-end architecture for LLM-driven trading with clear separation of contextual and low-latency modules; 2) a combined RL and convex optimization method that enforces CVaR constraints and transaction-cost awareness; and 3) a validated production-like deployment with hardware and communication design that meets real-time requirements.

Despite achieving strong results, the system has limitations: the dependency on curated news feeds and the need to validate LLM behavior under adversarial prompt manipulation are important concerns. The LLM embedding cadence trades off adaptability and latency and requires further study to optimize this balance. Future work will focus on three plans: (i) extending the framework to multi-asset FX portfolios and cross-asset hedging, (ii) integrating explainability modules to provide human-readable rationales for regulatory compliance, and (iii) evaluating adversarial robustness of LLM inputs and implementing prompt-verification pipelines. We hope this work encourages integration of modern language models into practical, auditable trading systems while emphasizing risk control and systems engineering best practices.
